help.intro: A smaller group of verbs builds its Perfekt with sein instead of haben — and English speakers, who have only 'have', get this wrong for years unless they learn the rule early. The rule is short: verbs of movement from one place to another (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, laufen, schwimmen, umziehen) and verbs of change of state (aufstehen, einschlafen, aufwachen, werden, sterben) take sein — plus three exceptions to learn by heart: sein (gewesen), bleiben (geblieben), passieren (passiert). Their participles are mostly irregular (gegangen, gefahren, gekommen, geworden). Everything else — including all verbs with an object — takes haben.
help.tips[0].title: Movers and changers take sein
help.tips[0].text: Movement A → B: gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, laufen, reisen, umziehen. Change of state: aufstehen, einschlafen, aufwachen, werden, sterben. Plus sein, bleiben, passieren.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: I went to Berlin and got up at seven.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: What happened? – Nothing, we stayed at home.
help.tips[0].trap: 'Ich habe gefahren' is the error. If the verb moves you or changes you, it takes sein.
help.tips[0].check.q: Letzten Sommer ____ wir nach Spanien geflogen.
help.tips[0].check.why: fliegen is movement from A to B, so it takes sein — and wir goes with sind.
help.tips[0].visual.root.q: Does the verb move you from A to B?
help.tips[0].visual.root.no.q: Does it describe a change of state (einschlafen, aufwachen, sterben)?
help.tips[0].visual.root.no.no.q: Is it sein, bleiben or passieren?
help.tips[1].title: The participles are mostly irregular
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: We went to the cinema and then walked home.
help.tips[1].check.q: Mein Bruder ist gestern spät nach Hause ____.
help.tips[1].check.why: kommen is irregular: the participle is gekommen, never gekommt.
help.tips[2].title: An object means haben — even for fahren
help.tips[2].text: Ich bin nach Köln gefahren (I travelled) but Ich habe das Auto gefahren (I drove the car). With a direct object the same verb switches to haben.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: He drove (went). – He drove the bus.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: We went to Hamburg. – My father drove the car.
help.tips[2].check.q: Meine Mutter ____ den neuen Wagen gefahren. (She drove the new car.)
help.tips[2].check.why: den neuen Wagen is a direct object, so fahren switches to haben.
help.tips[3].title: sein and bleiben: the two odd ones
help.tips[3].text: Ich bin in Rom gewesen, ich bin zwei Tage geblieben. In speech, war is preferred for 'was' (Ich war in Rom), but gewesen exists and you will read it.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: Have you ever been to Vienna? – Yes, I was there last year.
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: We stayed in Rome for three days.
help.tips[3].check.q: Wie lange ____ ihr in Paris geblieben?
help.tips[3].check.why: bleiben takes sein even though nobody moves — and ihr goes with seid.
help.remember[0]: Does the verb move you or change you? Then sein. Otherwise haben.
help.remember[1]: Three to memorise: gewesen, geblieben, passiert — all with sein.
help.context.en: On Saturday I got up early and took the train to Hamburg. My sister came too. We went for a walk at the harbour and to a concert in the evening. I didn't fall asleep until midnight! On Sunday we stayed at home – nothing happened.
help.mistakes[0].why: Movement from A to B takes sein.
help.mistakes[1].why: essen is not movement; it takes haben.
help.mistakes[2].why: The participle of a separable verb takes ge- in the middle.
help.hook: Went, came, stayed, fell asleep: verbs that move you or change you take sein — learn that one rule and your past tense sounds right.
help.recall.known: From "Perfekt: erste Schritte": fahren, bleiben and passieren take sein.
help.recall.today: The rule behind it: every verb of movement or change takes sein, and an object switches fahren back to haben.
help.table.caption: The verbs that take sein
sentences[0].why: Movement from A to B takes sein; fahren's participle is gefahren.
sentences[1].why: gehen moves you somewhere, so sein — and its participle is the irregular gegangen.
sentences[2].why: A change of state (lying → standing) takes sein; the separable prefix wraps the ge-: aufgestanden.
sentences[4].why: werden marks a change of state, so sein: geworden.
sentences[5].why: bleiben is the odd one out: no movement, yet it takes sein — geblieben.
sentences[6].why: Falling asleep is a change of state: sein, and the prefix wraps ge-: eingeschlafen.
sentences[7].why: fliegen is movement: sein + geflogen — ie → o.
sentences[9].why: schwimmen counts as movement: sein + geschwommen — i → o.
sentences[10].english: Have you ever been to Vienna? (in speech you will more often hear: Warst du schon einmal in Wien?)
sentences[10].why: sein is its own passenger: bin … gewesen — the participle nobody guesses.
sentences[11].english: She moved to Cologne last month.
sentences[11].why: Moving house is a change of place: sein, prefix around ge-: umgezogen.
sentences[12].why: passieren takes sein (something happened), and -ieren verbs take no ge-: passiert.
sentences[13].why: Waking is a change of state: sein — and aufwachen is regular: aufgewacht.
sentences[14].why: wandern is movement, so sein — and it is regular: gewandert.
sentences[15].why: Arriving is movement's end point: sein, prefix wraps ge-: angekommen.
sentences[16].why: Getting cold is becoming — werden takes sein: geworden.
sentences[17].english: Did you stay at the party long yesterday?
sentences[17].why: bleiben takes sein despite staying put — one of the exceptions to learn: geblieben.
